label: Leslie Kean
narrative: Leslie Kean is the person in this domain who took the government to court and won a search. On 31 January 2003 she filed a FOIA request with NASA for records referring to Kecksburg, the incident of 9 December 1965, the 'Fragology Files' for 1962-1967, Richard M. Schulherr, Project Moon Dust and Cosmos 96. NASA answered 'no records' on 11 April 2003. She appealed; NASA's Associate Deputy Administrator James Jennings granted the appeal on 18 June 2003 and promised an expedited agency-wide search; NASA then failed to act on its own letter, a failure the court later attributed to poor tracking and the relocation of the FOIA office. On 15 October 2003 she notified NASA she intended to sue, and on 9 December 2003 - thirty-eight years to the day after Kecksburg - she filed Kean v. National Aeronautics and Space Administration, Civil Action No. 03-2509 (EGS), in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, represented by Lobel, Novins & Lamont. Judge Emmet G. Sullivan held a hearing on 20 March 2007 and on 27 March 2007 issued a memorandum opinion finding that NASA had not met its burden of showing its searches were adequate, denying the agency summary judgment on the search question and ordering the parties to propose search and documentation procedures that would create a proper record. NASA settled in part on 16 October 2007 and searched under court supervision, filing joint status reports every sixty days until the case was dismissed on 24 August 2009. Kean went on to write 'UFOs: Generals, Pilots and Government Officials Go on the Record' (2010) and, with Ralph Blumenthal and Helene Cooper, the 16 December 2017 New York Times story that revealed AATIP.
